title: Looking back: the Japji
hook: thirty-eight pauris heard and understood, one by one

segments.voice: Yesterday, looking back at the practices: seva, kirtan, langar, simran, Nitnem, and your line, the practice that stuck. Did you do it again? Today, the longest climb of the year: the Japji. Day three hundred twenty-eight.

Here's something most people never do in their lives: read a whole scripture slowly, line by line, sound first and meaning second. You did that. For seventy-five days, camp four walked through Guru Nanak's Japji, the first words of the Guru Granth Sahib and the first prayer of a Sikh morning. You said the openings aloud, in Gurmukhi, even when your tongue tripped. Then you learned what they meant. Somewhere in the middle, it may have stopped feeling like homework. Today: looking back, at the Japji.
screen: `A WHOLE SCRIPTURE, SLOWLY.` → `SOUND FIRST, MEANING SECOND.` → `SEVENTY-FIVE DAYS.`

segments.voice: It began before the first pauri, with the Mool Mantar: Ik Onkar, Satnam, one Creator, whose name is truth, without fear, without hate, beyond time, never born, self-existent, known by the Guru's grace. Then the salok: true in the beginning, true through the ages, true now, and true forever. Then pauri one, and its first line, which you said aloud: sochai soch na hovaee je sochee lakh vaar. Thinking a hundred thousand times won't get you there. The way through is hukam, walking in the order. Then pauri two: everything comes by that order, and whoever understands it stops saying I, I. After that, the great runs. Suniai: by listening. Mannai: by trusting. Asankh: countless, countless prayers and countless fools, and Nanak unworthy to count them. Then the realms, one after another, like a ladder: duty, knowledge, effort, grace, and at the top, the realm of truth, where the Formless dwells. And pauri thirty-eight, the mint: jat paahaaraa dheeraj suniaar. Let restraint be the furnace and patience the goldsmith, and there the Word is minted. And last, the salok that closes it: pavan guru paanee pitaa maataa dharat mahat. Air the Guru, water the father, earth the great mother. From thinking you can't get there, to seeing the whole world as your family. That's the arc of the Japji. And here is the plain truth worth saying out loud: you read it. Many people who grew up hearing it every morning never went through it line by line. That's not a boast. It's a gift you gave yourself, one pauri at a time.
screen: `THE MOOL MANTAR AND AAD SACH.` · `PAURI 1: THINKING CAN'T REACH.` · `LISTENING, TRUSTING, THE REALMS.` · `THE MINT, AND AIR, WATER, EARTH.` · then, large: `I READ IT.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: read your favorite pauri. Settle, and think back through the Japji. Which pauri stayed with you? The first one, about overthinking? Listening? The countless? The mint? If you can, find it, and read it slowly, the Gurmukhi sound if you can manage it, then the meaning. If you can't look it up now, just say what you remember of it. Then sit with it, and let it be yours for a while. The bell holds the time.
Looking back. The Japji: Mool Mantar, thirty-eight pauris and the closing salok, heard and understood, one by one.
Your line: I read it. Today, tell one person, simply, that you read the Japji this year, and share the one line that stayed. Day three hundred twenty-eight.

howItsDone: Many Sikhs recite the Japji every morning as the first of the daily banis, from memory or from a gutka, and it opens the Guru Granth Sahib itself.

fork.setup: pauri one: you want to reach the truth, so you think about it a hundred thousand times. what does the Japji say?
options: thinking won't reach it; walk in the order, hukam.
fork.reveal: sochai soch na hovaee: thinking a hundred thousand times won't reach it. the way is walking in hukam.

original.note: Gurmukhi: japu, the title of Guru Nanak's Japji: recite, repeat, remember.

trapdoor: what you thought: the Japji is a long morning prayer.
what it means: a journey from 'thinking can't reach it' to seeing air, water and earth as family, one pauri at a time.
what a scholar hears: the Japji has the Mool Mantar, an opening salok, 38 pauris and a closing salok, on angs 1–8; the closing salok is also attributed to Guru Angad.
